items.prompt: Explain why a marketing objective states a measure, a quantity and a deadline.
items.canonical_answer: Because without them nobody can say whether it was met or use it to decide anything. "Sell more" gives the marketing department no guidance on which customers to aim at or what to charge, and at the end of the year any result at all can be called success. "Raise share from 12% to 15% within two years" does both jobs: it rules out decisions that cannot deliver it, and it is the standard the results are later judged against.

items.prompt: Analyse how a corporate objective of rapid growth changes what a business asks of its marketing department and of its other functions.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: senior managers adopt a corporate objective of raising revenue by 25% over three years. Marketing is then given an objective derived from it - a share rise, or entry into a second region - because those are the results marketing can deliver. To reach it, marketing has to aim at customers the business does not currently serve, which usually means new outlets, a wider promotional spend and possibly a changed price. Each of those commits the rest of the business: operations has to have the capacity to produce the extra output and the distribution to deliver it, human resources has to recruit and train the people to make and sell it, and finance has to fund the materials and the credit extended to new customers before any of the cash comes back. Where one of those is not in place, the orders are won and cannot be served, so the business loses the customers as well as the sales, and the corporate objective of growth is missed by a longer margin than if it had never been attempted. That is why functional objectives are agreed together rather than passed down one at a time.

items.prompt: A business is choosing between a marketing objective expressed as market share and one expressed as sales volume. Analyse what each choice commits the rest of the business to, and judge which is the safer objective for a business whose capacity is nearly full.
items.canonical_answer: A volume objective commits operations to producing a stated quantity, which the business can plan against because the number does not move. A share objective commits it to producing whatever quantity turns out to be the stated fraction of the market, which the business does not control: if the market grows 20%, holding share alone requires 20% more output, and gaining share requires more again. For a business already near capacity, the share objective therefore carries a risk the volume objective does not - it can be missed because the market grew, or met at the cost of orders that cannot be produced. The counterargument is that share is the better measure of competitiveness, because a volume target can be met in a growing market while rivals take customers away. The safer choice here is a volume objective with a share figure reported alongside it: the commitment stays inside what capacity can deliver, and the share figure still shows whether the position is being lost. That judgement reverses once the capacity constraint is removed.

items.prompt: Explain how a rise in the cost of imported inputs affects the quantity a business is willing to supply.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism runs through profitability at the existing price. A rise in input cost means each unit produced leaves less for the business at the price it is currently charging, so producing the same quantity is worth less than it was. Businesses tend to respond by offering less at that price - cutting production runs, dropping the least profitable lines, or delaying orders - unless they can pass the cost on in a higher price or reduce the cost some other way. How far supply actually falls depends on how much of the rise customers will absorb and on how quickly the business can change what it makes.

items.prompt: A maize miller in Otjiwarongo faces a poor national harvest and, in the same month, a rise in the wages it pays its packers. Explain how these two events affect its market in different ways.
items.canonical_answer: The poor harvest raises the price the miller pays for grain and reduces how much grain it can obtain at all, so the quantity it can supply falls whatever it would like to sell. This is a supply-side event that affects every miller buying from the same harvest, so the market price of maize meal tends to rise. The wage rise is also a cost, but it affects this miller alone unless competitors face the same increase; it reduces what the miller keeps at the current price and so reduces the quantity it is willing to supply, but it does not change what rivals can offer. Demand for maize meal is unchanged by either event, so the miller's customers face a higher price for a staple they still need, and the miller may find volumes hold better than they would for a product households can do without.

items.prompt: Explain how excess demand at the current price tends to push that price upwards.
items.canonical_answer: Where customers want more at the current price than sellers are offering, stock runs down and some customers go unserved. Sellers discover that they can raise the price without losing the sale, because there is a queue behind the customer who refuses, and some of them do. Other sellers follow once they see it. items.prompt: Analyse the effect on the price and on the quantity traded when supply falls while demand is unchanged, and explain how a business can tell that case apart from a rise in demand.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: a drought cuts the quantity of beef that processors can obtain, while households want exactly as much as before. Less is offered at the current price than customers want to buy, so stocks run down, sellers find they can raise the price, and the price rises. The higher price discourages some buyers, so the quantity actually traded settles lower than before: the market clears at a higher price and a smaller volume. Now compare a rise in demand with supply unchanged. Customers want more at the current price, the same shortage appears, and the price rises again - but here suppliers respond by offering more, so the quantity traded settles higher than before. The price moves the same way in both cases; the quantity moves in opposite directions, and that is the signal a business reads. A butcher seeing prices and volumes both rising is looking at stronger demand and can plan to buy and sell more. A butcher seeing prices rise while volumes fall is looking at a supply problem, and the right response is to secure supply and manage customers' expectations rather than to expand. Reading it the wrong way round commits the business to volumes it cannot obtain.

items.prompt: Analyse how selling into export markets changes the risks carried by a Namibian manufacturer that currently sells only at home.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: a manufacturer with all its sales in Namibia decides to sell into Angola, Zambia and South Africa. The first effect is that its revenue no longer depends on one country's economy, so a Namibian downturn that would previously have cut its sales in full now cuts only part of them - the business has spread the risk it already carried. Against that it takes on risks it did not have. Goods travel further, so more capital sits in transit and a delay at a border becomes a delay in payment. Each market has its own rules on labelling, standards and import duty, and failing one of them can hold a consignment at the frontier. And sales made in another currency can be worth less in N$ by the time they are paid, so a contract signed at a profit can be settled at a loss without anything going wrong commercially. The net effect on the business is that revenue becomes more stable across countries and less predictable in amount, and the finance function has to plan for longer cash cycles - which is why exporters often price in a margin for currency movement rather than at their domestic margin.

items.prompt: Namib Cable sells wiring harnesses to two vehicle assemblers, which take 80% of its output, and boxed jump leads to hardware shops. Explain why the harness side of the business is more exposed to events it does not control.
items.canonical_answer: The harness side sells into an industrial market with two buyers, each worth about 40% of output, and the demand is derived: the assemblers order as many harnesses as their own vehicle sales require. If vehicle sales in the region fall by a quarter, Namib Cable's harness orders fall by roughly the same proportion however good its quality, price and service are, because nothing it does can make its customer sell more vehicles. Losing one of the two customers outright would remove about 40% of output at a stroke. The jump-lead side sells into a consumer market with thousands of small buyers, so no single customer's decision moves the total much, and demand comes from households whose need arises from their own vehicles rather than from another business's sales. The exposure is therefore concentration plus derived demand on one side, and neither on the other.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between product orientation and customer orientation.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is the order of two questions. A product-oriented business asks what it can make well, and then who will buy it. A customer-oriented business asks what customers want, and then whether it can make it. items.prompt: Analyse how a strongly product-oriented approach can lead a business to launch a product that does not sell.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: an engineering firm decides to develop the most durable water pump it can build, because durability is what its engineers are good at. Design decisions are then taken to serve that goal: heavier materials, a longer-lasting motor, a higher specification than anything else on the market. Each of those raises the cost of making the pump, and the price has to follow. Because no customer need was checked first, the business does not know until launch whether the buyers it is aiming at - smallholders replacing a pump every few years - value durability enough to pay the difference, and if they are choosing mainly on the price they can afford this month, they do not. The result is stock that does not move, development money already spent, and a price that cannot be cut far because the cost is built into the design. The effect on the business is a loss that is discovered late and is expensive to correct, since redesigning the product costs almost as much as developing it did. The same approach can succeed where the technical lead is genuine and customers cannot describe what they have never seen, which is why the risk is about unchecked assumptions rather than about engineering.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to treat customer orientation as a way of removing the risk of a failed launch?
items.canonical_answer: Because it reduces that risk rather than removing it. Research can be badly designed, the people asked may not represent the buyers, the answers given to a researcher can differ from what those people later pay for, and a market can move between the research and the launch. Customer orientation checks the need before the money is committed, which is why it is usually the safer order, but the check itself can be wrong. Treating it as a removal of risk leads a business to skip the smaller safeguards - a limited launch, a test area - that catch a research error before it becomes a national one.

items.prompt: Explain why a rising market share may strengthen a business's position with its suppliers and its retailers.
items.canonical_answer: Because a rising share means it is buying more from the one and offering more turnover to the other. A supplier selling larger and more regular quantities to the same customer may be willing to improve the price or the credit terms to keep that business, since losing it would now cost more. A retailer allocates shelf space to products that sell, so a business whose share is rising has a stronger case for more space or better placing, which in turn supports further sales. Neither response is certain - a supplier with more demand than capacity has less reason to concede - but both become more likely as the business becomes more important to the other party.

items.prompt: Analyse how a business can increase its sales every year and still be losing market share.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: a business raises its sales by 8% in a year in which its market grows by 20%. Its own figures look healthy - more units, more revenue, a busier factory - but the market grew two and a half times faster, so the extra customers went mostly to somebody else and its share has fallen. The mechanism is that a growing market attracts new entrants and encourages existing rivals to expand, so growth that looks like an opportunity is also an invitation to competitors. The consequence is that the business ends the year with more revenue and a weaker position: fewer of the market's customers, less bargaining weight with retailers, and rivals whose larger volumes may let them make each unit more cheaply. The effect on the business shows up later rather than now - when the market stops growing, the sales that were coming from market growth stop coming, and a business that never won customers from rivals has no source of growth left. That is why share is read alongside sales rather than instead of it.

An industrial product is promoted through personal selling, trade fairs, trade publications and technical demonstrations, because the buyers are few and can be named, so the seller can reach each of them directly and answer the technical questions a specification raises. Distribution follows the same logic: industrial products move more often direct from producer to customer, consumer products more often through wholesalers and retailers.

Both sides must be described, with the reason - the number of buyers - made clear.
Distribution may be credited as a further difference.

items.prompt: Analyse how having a few large customers rather than many small ones changes the way a business markets itself.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: a manufacturer's ten largest customers account for most of its output. Because each is worth a large share of revenue, losing one is not a rounding error but a material fall in turnover, so the value of retaining each customer is far higher than the value of reaching an additional stranger. That changes where the marketing money goes: from advertising aimed at an anonymous audience to account management, technical support, negotiated contracts and reliable delivery, all of which are aimed at named people the seller can visit. It also changes the shape of the selling effort, since the buyer is a group - a user, a technical assessor, a buyer and a finance approver - each with a different question, so the seller prepares different material for each rather than one message. The consequence for the business is a lower promotional cost per N$ of sales and a much higher exposure to a single customer's decision, so the same concentration that makes marketing cheap makes revenue fragile. Businesses in that position usually try to add customers to spread the risk, which is a marketing objective that comes from the structure of the market rather than from ambition.

items.prompt: Explain why personal selling is used more in business-to-business markets than in consumer markets.
items.canonical_answer: Because the buyers are few enough to visit and each order is large enough to justify the visit. A salesperson calling on twenty industrial buyers can reach most of that market in a month, which is impossible where the buyers are fifty thousand households. The cost of the visit is small against an order worth several hundred thousand N$, while the same cost against a single household purchase would be absurd.

items.prompt: A Namibian brewery sells a standard lager nationwide and a small-batch craft beer through a few Windhoek restaurants. Explain the difference between the features of mass marketing and niche marketing, using the brewery's two beers.
items.canonical_answer: Mass marketing aims one standardised product at a large market; niche marketing aims a specialised product at a small, identified group. The standard lager shows the mass-market features: large volumes, wide distribution through bottle stores and bars, promotion through media that reach large audiences, and competition that turns largely on price. The craft beer shows the niche features: small volumes, a distinctive product, promotion aimed at restaurant diners who seek it out, a price that reflects the specialism, and few direct rivals. The trade-off behind both is that standardising makes volume possible, while specialising allows a higher price but limits how much can be sold.

items.prompt: Analyse why a business serving a niche market usually has a higher cost of making each unit than one serving a mass market.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the niche business sells small volumes of a specialised product, and the mass marketer sells large volumes of a standardised one. Because the niche business makes fewer units, the cost of designing the product, setting up the machinery and running the business is carried by a smaller number of them, so each unit carries more of it. Its production runs are short, so time is lost changing over between batches rather than producing, and it buys materials in small quantities, which usually means paying more for each unit of material than a buyer taking a container-load. The consequence is a higher cost for each unit produced, which is why the niche business needs the higher price its specialism allows - the margin per unit, not the volume, is what has to cover its costs. The effect on the business is that its position depends on customers continuing to value the specialism: if they stop, it is left with a high cost per unit and no premium to carry it, which is the risk built into the strategy rather than a failure of management.

items.prompt: Explain one disadvantage of serving a mass market.
items.canonical_answer: The capital has to be committed before the revenue arrives. Capacity to produce at volume, stock in wide distribution and promotion heavy enough to be noticed all have to be paid for in advance, and the business finds out only afterwards whether the demand it planned for is there. That matters beyond the money: having spent it, the business is built around one standardised product, so if customers move it cannot change direction quickly, and the same capacity that made it efficient makes it slow. Competition from other large sellers then tends to hold prices down, so the margin that is meant to repay the investment is under pressure from the start.

items.canonical_answer: Eight machinists cannot produce at the volume a mass clothing market needs, and N$200 000 will not buy the capacity or the promotion to be noticed against importers already competing on price there. Entering that market would mean a cost per garment above the importers' and no money left to tell anyone the business exists. A niche is within reach: school uniforms for a group of schools, or workwear for a mining contractor, are orders eight machinists can fill, the customers can be approached directly without advertising, and buyers who need a specific garment may accept a price that reflects it. The higher margin on each garment is what makes the small volume viable. The risk to accept is concentration - losing one contract would be serious - so the business should be working towards a second and third customer from the start.

items.prompt: A niche furniture maker with 30 employees, a full order book and N$1 400 000 of retained cash is considering moving into the mass furniture market with a standardised range. Evaluate whether it should do so.
items.canonical_answer: It should not make the move as a switch, though it may make it as an addition. The decisive criterion is whether the business can hold a cost per unit low enough to compete on price in a market where price is what competition turns on, and nothing in its position suggests it can: 30 employees and N$1 400 000 buy neither the capacity nor the promotion that established mass producers already have, and the skills that make its niche furniture worth a premium - fitting, finishing, customer contact - are exactly the costs a standardised range has to remove. The strongest argument the other way is real: the niche caps its revenue, the order book is already full, so growth has to come from somewhere, and a full order book is the safest moment to attempt something risky. That argues for using the cash to widen the niche, or to test a simplified range through existing customers while the specialist work continues to pay the wages. The judgement reverses if the business can find a segment of the wider market that still values what it is good at - hotel or office contracts, for instance, where durability and fitting matter and buyers are not choosing on price alone. The condition for any move is that the specialist business keeps funding it until the new range covers its own costs.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that a business serving a niche market should be regarded as being in a weaker position than one serving a mass market.
items.canonical_answer: The view is wrong as a general rule, and what makes it wrong is its sweep. A niche business is weaker on some dimensions and stronger on others, and which matters depends on the business and the market. It is weaker on revenue available, on cost per unit, and on its exposure to one group of customers. It is stronger on margin per unit, on closeness to its customers, and on the capital it needs to start - and a mass marketer carries risks a niche business does not, since its capital is committed to capacity that cannot be redirected quickly if demand moves. The decisive criterion is what the business can actually finance and produce: a firm without the capital to build capacity and buy national promotion is not in a stronger position by aiming at a mass market, it is simply in a market it cannot serve. The strongest argument for the view is that a large competitor can enter a profitable niche and take it, which is a genuine vulnerability. That is a condition rather than a rule: it depends on whether the niche is large enough to interest a mass producer and whether what the niche business does can be copied at volume. Where the specialism rests on skill, reputation or local knowledge, entry is harder than the view assumes.

items.prompt: Analyse what happens to a business that segments its market on a basis which does not divide how its customers buy.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: a household-cleaning brand divides its market by age, because the data was available, in a market where age has little to do with which cleaner a household buys. The division itself is tidy - every customer falls into one group - so the business proceeds as if it had found something. It then incurs the costs of segmenting: separate packaging, separate advertising for each age group, and shorter production runs on more variants, which raises the cost of making each unit. Because the groups do not differ in what they buy, the separate campaigns reach people who would have responded to the general one, so the extra spending produces no extra sales. The consequence is a higher cost base carried by the same revenue, and a marketing budget divided into pieces too small to be noticed in any one group. The effect on the business is worse than doing nothing, because it now believes it understands its market and may repeat the exercise on the same basis. The test that would have prevented it is whether the chosen variable explains different buying, not whether it sorts customers neatly.

items.prompt: A dairy selling one flavour of drinking yoghurt nationally is considering launching four flavours aimed at four different groups of customers. Evaluate whether it should segment its market in this way.
items.canonical_answer: It should segment only if it can answer three questions first, and on the evidence given it has answered none of them. The decisive criterion is whether the differences between the proposed groups are large enough to change what customers will buy or pay: four flavours divide the product, but unless those groups actually want different flavours, the business has created four production runs to sell the same total quantity. The second question is size - each group has to be big enough to cover the extra cost of packaging, distribution and promotion for its own flavour - and the third is reach, since a distinct flavour is useless if the dairy cannot get a different message to the group that wants it. The strongest argument for going ahead is real: one flavour nationally is a compromise product, and a rival that segments first may take the customers whose preference is not being met, which is how small entrants get into markets held by large sellers. So the judgement is conditional rather than negative. The dairy should test two flavours in one region before committing to four nationally, because the test answers the three questions at a fraction of the cost of being wrong. If the test shows the groups buying the same volume of whatever is on the shelf, the answer is to keep one flavour and spend the money on price or distribution instead.

The record also shows what a customer has not bought, which is where a related product can be offered to somebody who has already trusted the business once, and that is an easier sale than the first one was. items.prompt: Etosha Paints sold N$40 000 000 of decorative paint two years ago and N$42 000 000 last year. The Namibian decorative paint market was worth N$200 000 000 two years ago and N$262 500 000 last year. Calculate Etosha's market share in each year and the market growth over the period; then evaluate whether the board should set next year's marketing objective in terms of sales or in terms of market share.
items.canonical_answer:
Share two years ago: N$40 000 000 / N$200 000 000 = 20%. Share last year: N$42 000 000 / N$262 500 000 = 16%. Market growth: the market rose by N$262 500 000 - N$200 000 000 = N$62 500 000, and N$62 500 000 / N$200 000 000 = 31.25%. Etosha's own sales rose by N$2 000 000, which is 5%.

What the figures show: the business grew and lost position. Almost all of the N$62 500 000 of extra demand went to competitors or new entrants, so while the market keeps growing Etosha can report higher sales each year and still be getting weaker.

Judgement: the objective should be set in terms of market share. The decisive criterion is which measure reveals the problem the board has just discovered - a sales objective was met last year while the business lost four percentage points of share, so setting another one would hide the same failure again. A share objective forces the marketing department to win customers from rivals rather than wait for market growth to carry it. The strongest argument against is that share is not fully within the department's control: if the market grows 31% again, holding 16% means producing 31% more paint, and Etosha may not have the capacity, so a share target can be missed for reasons that have nothing to do with marketing. The condition is therefore that the share objective is agreed with operations and finance before it is set, and that it is expressed with a sales floor beneath it - for example, hold share at 16% and raise sales by at least 20% - so that the department is not rewarded for a share gained in a shrinking market.

items.prompt: Kavango Solar sells home solar kits to 4 200 households across five regions and records each installation. It has N$600 000 to spend and two proposals: segment its market and run four separate campaigns, or install a CRM system to sell servicing and upgrades to its existing customers. Analyse both proposals and evaluate which it should fund.
items.canonical_answer:
Proposal one, segmentation. Kavango's five regions differ in climate, grid connection and income, so a geographic and demographic division is available at low cost, and the campaigns could be aimed where off-grid households actually are rather than at the whole country. The test is whether those differences change what customers buy: a household with no grid connection buys a larger system than one topping up a supply, so here the basis does divide buying, and the segmentation is likely to raise the proportion of the audience with a reason to respond. The cost is four campaigns instead of one and the research to define them.

Proposal two, CRM. The business already records every installation, which is most of the data a CRM system needs, and 4 200 customers is a base small enough to keep accurate. Solar kits need servicing and batteries need replacing, so these customers do buy again - the condition that decides most CRM cases is satisfied. The record identifies which household has which kit and when it was fitted, so servicing and upgrade offers can be timed to the need.

Recommendation: fund the CRM proposal. The decisive criterion is which spend has the shorter and more certain path to revenue. Selling servicing and batteries to 4 200 households who already trust the business converts far better than persuading new households to buy a first system, and the data is already being collected, so most of the cost is in using it rather than gathering it. The strongest argument the other way is that 4 200 customers is a small base to build revenue growth on, and segmented campaigns reach the much larger number of households that have never bought - which is where long-term growth has to come from. items.prompt: A wholesaler of building materials in Windhoek has seen the price it pays for cement rise 18% in four months while the quantity available to it has fallen. Identify the questions it should ask about its market before deciding how to respond, and explain what each one tells it.
items.canonical_answer:
Has the quantity traded in the market risen or fallen? This separates the two explanations. Price up with volume up points to stronger demand, and the response is to secure more stock and consider raising the price. Price up with volume down points to a supply restriction, and the response is different: secure supply and manage customers rather than expand.

What has happened on the supply side? Input costs, energy, a plant out of action, an import problem or a change in duty each affect how long the restriction lasts. A plant under repair resolves; a permanent duty does not.

What has happened to its customers? Construction demand follows building activity, so the wholesaler should ask whether its own customers' order books are growing. If they are, demand is part of the story and the price will hold.

Can the cost be passed on? That depends on what competitors are charging and on whether customers have an alternative supplier. Where every wholesaler faces the same cost, more of it can be passed on than where one has stock bought earlier.

How long will the position last? A temporary restriction argues for holding prices and protecting long-standing customers, since the business gets the relationship back when supply returns. A lasting one argues for repricing now and accepting lower volumes.

items.canonical_answer: First, work out from the records which treatments recur on a known interval - vaccinations, dosing, herd testing - and contact each farmer before the date rather than waiting for the call. The visit is needed either way; the practice that asks first gets the work, and a farmer reminded in time is spared a problem rather than sold a service. Second, use the records to see which clients have stopped calling. A farm that used to call monthly and has not called for six months has either lost stock or moved to another practice, and a telephone call while the position is recoverable costs nothing against the value of a herd client. Both changes use information the practice already holds and neither requires new promotion.

items.prompt: A furniture retailer with one store in Windhoek sells nationally by delivery. It is considering dividing its marketing budget between four regions and advertising separately in each. Evaluate whether it should segment its market geographically in this way.
items.canonical_answer: It should not, in the form proposed. The decisive criterion is whether location changes what these customers buy or how they can be reached, and for delivered furniture sold from one store it largely does not: a sofa bought in Rundu is the same sofa bought in Windhoek, ordered through the same channel, and the customer's decision turns on price, range and delivery cost rather than on where they live. Splitting one budget four ways would leave four campaigns too small to be noticed rather than one that is. There is a real argument the other way, and it is about reach rather than needs: delivery cost and time do differ by region, regional radio reaches audiences that national media miss, and if the retailer has almost no customers in two of the four regions, a campaign aimed there could open markets the Windhoek store never touches. That points to a different division of the money - a national campaign plus one regional test in the weakest region - rather than to an even four-way split. The judgement reverses if the retailer opens branches: a store in each region gives each one a catchment, a delivery radius and a local competitor, and at that point the regions are genuinely different markets.

Context: the judgement must rest on the facts given.
Criterion: name the decisive factor.
Counterargument: address the strongest argument on the other side.
Condition: state what would change the answer.

items.prompt: A magazine publisher launching a personal-finance title has N$90 000 for research. Evaluate whether it should spend it on demographic profiling of possible readers or on psychographic research into their attitudes to money.
items.canonical_answer: It should spend most of it on psychographic research and buy the demographic profile cheaply alongside. The decisive criterion is which body of data the publisher cannot obtain any other way: age, income and occupation for the Namibian population are already available in census and official statistics at little cost, so paying N$90 000 for them buys a tidier version of something largely in the public domain. Attitudes to saving, to debt and to financial advice are not published anywhere and are exactly what decides whether somebody buys a personal-finance magazine - two readers on the same salary may differ entirely, one wanting help with debt and the other with investing, and those are different magazines. The strongest argument for the demographic spend is practical: advertising is bought and sold in demographic terms, so a title that cannot describe its readers by age and income will struggle to sell space to advertisers, and advertising revenue may matter more than cover price. That is why the recommendation is a split rather than a choice - commission the attitude research, and record enough demographic detail in the same study to describe the segments it finds in the terms advertisers use. The judgement would change if the publisher already held attitude data from an existing title, in which case the gap to fill is the demographic one.
